rewrites.0477B194: The plan follows one chain from vision to measure. Each level answers a different question. The goal says what must change and the objective says where; the initiative says what Wesgro and its partners do and the indicator says how Steerco will know it has happened (section 5.1).
rewrites.7EE427F2: Seven levels run from the vision to the measures. Each has a fixed count in this plan. One vision says where the province is going: grow international arrivals from 1.5 million in 2025 towards 2.5 million by 2035. Three goals say what must change, such as Reshape demand. Six themes say in which part of the system, such as source market growth and diversification. Twenty objectives say where the evidence says to act, such as Convert India and China hub traffic. Eighteen initiatives say what Wesgro and its partners do, such as I4 India and China hub conversion. The 146 actions say who does what, by tier, such as activation inside Xiaohongshu, Douyin and MakeMyTrip. The indicators, 8 at impact, 31 at outcome and 41 at output level, say how Steerco knows, such as T2-06 India and China hub arrivals. The counts come from Chapter 3, the action tables and the traceability table in Appendix A1.
rewrites.6DBF2A40: Eighteen initiatives cover the twenty objectives. Eleven of them are in implementation by 2028. Thirteen draw mainly on Wesgro's operating budget (section 4.6).
rewrites.2972B07E: Three phases run to 2035. The first is weighted to conversion and seat retention, with the green-season calendar and the inclusion pilots beside them.
rewrites.693DCFF8: Phase 1 works on the levers that move before the airport can, inside existing mandates and budgets. Stakeholder agreements on roles and accountabilities are in place for each initiative in 2027 (section 4.4). Conversion work starts at once: dated reasons to travel, safety reassurance, regional information on each market's platforms and the green-season calendar (I1, I2, I3). The Cape Town Air Access partnership is re-termed to hold and add seats on the full routes and to open new routes outside the peak hours (I6). The I3 audit follows regional product from discovery to sale and prepares a bounded support trial. Two or three inclusion pilots start (I12). Steerco, the data-sharing protocol and the escalation agenda start in the first quarter (I15, I16, I17), because every other initiative reports through them.
rewrites.3EAA801F: Phase 2 scales what Phase 1 proved. Hub conversion, regional Africa and segment marketing run at scale. Corridor mobility and product move from design to delivery, on the Garden Route, the Cape Winelands and the Overberg first. The quality charter is adopted and phased by district. The investment pipeline reaches financial close on its first projects. Flow management extends beyond the two pilot sites where the pilots held. The safety pathway widens if the 2028 review supports it. The mid-term review in 2030 tests seat growth against the path the target requires and checks that the runway is on its published dates (section 5.6).
rewrites.39C3394A: Every charter uses the same fields. It states the aim, the objectives served, the convenor, the key stakeholders and the tier of government. It then sets the actions in each phase (marked Design or Implement) and closes with the dependencies, the funding route, the risks and the indicators it moves. Actions come from the Chapter 3 action tables. Each charter opens with the 2027 stakeholder agreement. Rand bands are still to be set (section 4.6).
rewrites.4644B08B: Raise value per visitor from the mature markets and target every priority market by segment, not by country alone. Build recognition of the regions (and nights spent there) beside city conversion.
rewrites.191B7263: Agree (2027): convene the stakeholders and agree roles and accountabilities. Design (2027): segment targets inside each priority market; a shared segment frame with SA Tourism, the City and Cape Town Tourism; destination-specific segment research; tests of three brand presentations; regional product, inventory links and completed regional bookings written into campaign and airline agreements. Also in 2027: dated reasons to travel and safety reassurance in campaigns; an extension strategy agreed with US and UK safari and tour operators. Implement (2028): move spend from broad awareness to trade-led conversion; luxury-advisor and high-end operator distribution in the UK, USA, Germany, France and Switzerland.
rewrites.37099D2B: Build an April to September demand spine from business events and flagship weeks (with May to August as the first winter portfolio) and sell it with the seats.
rewrites.038EC7E4: T1-05; T2-02 ICCA meetings and bids secured, against Wesgro's 161 over FY26 to FY30, T2-03 April to September seat share; T3-03 calendar published; T3-04 all bids submitted and those for May to September events.
rewrites.411A6A11: Put the province beyond Cape Town where each market plans, with the information a traveller needs to commit. Make regional product found and sold where travellers book.
rewrites.31BC25C5: Convert the Indian and Chinese travellers already flying in through hubs and prepare the direct route case for when runway capacity arrives.
rewrites.726FFDF3: Hold calls above Wesgro's 250 over FY26 to FY30 by making the regional circuit work for lines. Grow shore spend through call-day capacity beyond the flagship sites and regional day stops.
rewrites.2EDD6344: Investor engagement; first projects at financial close; one levy case for the visitor economy, set against its legal route and timing; blended finance tested with DEDAT, the Department of Mobility and the City.
rewrites.4DB1A0ED: Four levers sit outside the province and cannot be bought or marketed into place. Route rights and visas sit with the national tier, the airport and port capital programmes with national SOEs and policing with SAPS. The plan treats them as an escalation agenda (I17), carried by Steerco through DEDAT to the national departments and SOEs. The plan proposes that Wesgro's Advocacy and Advisory unit, set up to build evidence-based policy feedback on levers the province does not control, runs it day to day. DEDAT's visa study supplies its visa asks, already ranked. The asks now start from ETA performance data that only Home Affairs holds. Each item is stated as a decision, the body that holds it and a date the province is asking for. Wesgro's own route work (I6) runs inside the existing agreements meanwhile.[^417]
rewrites.33F10944: The Province also holds three roles the plan now relies on. On safety, DEDAT funds the City's Tourist and Visitor Safety Unit, runs the Tourism Safety and Support service and convenes the Provincial Tourism Safety Forum (I17). The Province holds oversight of policing and SAPS keeps command. On red tape, DEDAT's Red Tape Reduction service carries the tourism case route and records where approvals stall (I14). On procurement, the plan asks DEDAT and the Provincial Treasury for the practice note that lets municipalities buy LTO services lawfully (I12).
rewrites.0AE9968B: Municipalities and LTOs hold the assets, the selling bodies and the visitor services that the regional and inclusion initiatives depend on. The plan proposes to engage them on the community selling bodies in the pilots (I12), on covenants for public assets (I12, I14) and on the route and product work in their districts (I3, I9). The City of Cape Town is a stakeholder in segments, events, routes, cruise, mobility, product, flagship sites, community pilots and safety (I1, I2, I6 to I9, I11, I12, I17). Cape Town Tourism is a stakeholder in segments, routes and data (I1, I6, I16). The plan proposes both for Steerco. The City's framework for 2019 to 2024 set out three plans the initiatives can build on: an air, rail and cruise access programme, a Cape Town+ offer and a Tourist Safety Programme. The safety services run today, through the City's Tourist and Visitor Safety Unit and its 24/7 visitor-support service. MFMA Circular No. 131 interrupted established municipal funding of LTOs. Municipalities can still buy LTO services through procurement (section 2.5; I12).[^418]
rewrites.3EA8155F: Fourteen actions can start by mid-2028, eleven of them inside Wesgro's current mandate and budget. Each one opens a market, a baseline or a seat that a later initiative needs.
rewrites.2231B3CF: Put dated reasons to travel and current safety information into campaigns and publish regional itineraries and visitor information on each market's platforms
rewrites.5D1EE07F: Request carrying capacity from the flagship sites (to publish beside the Treasury's 2023 visitor counts) and start a costed condition register
rewrites.7248D326: Give each pilot community one live booking route and paid departures with buyer commitments, before any promotion
rewrites.2E65A75B: Most of the plan runs on budgets that already exist [[QUERY Q25: is new public money sought in Phase 1?]]. The capital it needs sits with ACSA, PRASA, Transnet and private investors. None of it has been costed yet.
rewrites.0CD22654: No deliverable costs any initiative [[QUERY Q1: cost of the plan and who pays?]]. The Inception Report scoped an investment opportunity framework with return scoring, but no separate output was delivered. Stakeholders describe Western Cape tourism funding as materially below peer destinations without giving a figure.[^419] This section leaves the rand bands to be set with Wesgro Finance and DEDAT before the plan is signed off [[QUERY Q2: rand bands due before sign-off or before Gate 1?]].
rewrites.2B468B9E: The initiatives table in section 4.1 gives each initiative's main and supporting funding routes. Current allocations show where the plan's money sits today. DEDAT's 2026/27 main budget is R596.765 million, including a R127.355 million transfer to Wesgro and R6.8 million for the CTICC. It earmarks R3 million for tourism safety and R4 million for tourism growth initiatives. The department's performance plan carries a R7 million Tourism Growth Fund. These are existing allocations, not spare money. The MyCiTi operating grant ends in 2027/28, so the airport link needs a funded service specification before any product is sold on it (I8).
rewrites.1BFAF41B: Thirteen initiatives draw mainly on Wesgro's operating budget and four need private capital as a main source. Wesgro Finance and DEDAT agree a stop list before Gate 1, naming the Wesgro work deprioritised to fund the initiatives (section 4.8).
rewrites.1A82C0BA: **Crowding in capital.** The rule for capital is the Inclusion Plan's: invest after demand is shown and attach a maintenance and marketing covenant to any public asset. Wesgro's investment promotion work builds the tourism pipeline from the Infrastructure Report's gap-closure tables, where every district lists tourism gaps with no committed capital (I14). Route support runs through the Cape Town Air Access partnership, scaled and re-termed with public and private money (I6) [[QUERY Q26: source of the added route support?]]. Its funders already sit in the partnership: the City, the province, ACSA, Cape Town Tourism, SA Tourism, Wesgro and private-sector partners [[QUERY Q15: partnership or unit?]]. Its support carries resilience conditions, from tapering and matched airline marketing to clawbacks (objective 7). Corridor mobility (I8) bids into the provincial transport budget; the draft land transport framework allocates R22.8 billion to transport initiatives in the 2024 MTEF. The same framework plans a tourist levy case, which I14 would widen to cover destination management.[^420]
rewrites.25284FE7: **What the SLA asks and what is still to do.** The SLA asks for return projections on infrastructure priorities (clause 1.1.8.3). Those need costed projects. The only costed items in hand are the airport, rail and port programmes the province does not fund. The return case is therefore an output of I14 in Phase 1, built project by project as the pipeline forms.
rewrites.794D52B1: **Programme office.** A small office inside Wesgro runs the plan on a build, operate and transfer basis. It builds the charters, the dashboard and the reporting calendar in Phase 1, runs them through Phase 2 and hands them to the line units by the end of 2031. It owns the scorecard and the dashboard. Wesgro Research owns the indicator definitions and the data protocol (I16).
rewrites.59073472: Four decision points test the plan against its indicators. Each one decides what the next phase funds.
rewrites.54F7F820: Move to Expand; scale or stop each pilot; renew, change or stop the I3 support trial; extend or stop flow management at the pilot sites; widen or hold the safety pathway; confirm route cases for India and China and bring them into Phase 2 if ACSA awards the runway contract on its December 2029 schedule
rewrites.0A1434B0: Sixteen risks could move the plan off its path. The two rated high on both measures concern the national air regime and the Gulf hubs.
rewrites.4C28711A: The chain follows the theory of change in Figure 1.2: outputs lead to outcomes and outcomes to impact, only where its assumptions hold.
rewrites.6BB05150: Goal 1 initiatives (I1 to I5) move arrivals, market mix, spend and green-season nights. Goal 2 initiatives (I6 to I11) move seats, cruise volumes and the share of visitors and spend outside the Metro. Goal 3 initiatives (I12 to I18) move community spend and jobs and supply the governance and data every other indicator relies on.
rewrites.524C0110: Tier 1 measures the 2035 case and is reported to the Board. Tier 2 measures the objectives (one to three each) and is reported to Steerco each quarter where the source allows. Tier 3 measures the initiatives' own outputs and is reported by the convenors to the programme office each month. The full register, with targets, sits in the toolkit (section 5.7).
rewrites.6271C7BF: Overseas visitor nights in April to September and their share of the year, reported beside peak-season volume
rewrites.7A308833: Thirty-one Tier 2 indicators give each objective one to three outcome measures. Twelve of them take their baseline in 2027.
rewrites.3F0C80DF: Green-season calendar published; all bids submitted and those for May to September events
rewrites.4F7BC4A5: Baselines are fixed at 2025, the growth model's base year, for the growth-model indicators and at FY2024/25 for the airport series, the recovery baseline used in Chapter 2. Targets follow two cases: the base case, which assumes Wesgro's current activity continues with hub carriers adding capacity; the accelerated case, which adds direct India and China routes and dedicated activation. The model gives the base case for 2028, 2030, 2032, 2034 and 2035. It gives the other cases for 2035 only. The 2031 base value and the accelerated milestones are computed and marked as such.[^423]
rewrites.08D33A44: **Arrivals.** The model's 2025 base and the airport series measure different things: arrivals on the growth model's basis, which is still to be confirmed (Appendix A2); international passenger arrivals at Cape Town International. The airport series is the quarterly proxy because ACSA publishes it. It stood at 1.44 million in FY24/25 and 1.57 million in FY25/26. Both are reported, each against its own history.[^424]
rewrites.4916BC6E: **Spread and community spend.** No deliverable reports district visitor spend. The Provincial Treasury's district reviews give tourist spend as a share of GDPR, from 6.7% in the Metro to 16.8% on the West Coast in 2023. That measures tourism's weight in each district economy, not where provincial visitor spend lands. The share outside the Metro therefore takes its baseline from the data protocol in 2027 (I16). T1-06 carries no interim level before then. The community share starts from the Inclusion Plan's traced floor; its 1% is a reference point that plan gives, not a target any party has adopted.[^429]
rewrites.154A7360: Stakeholders put data among the top barriers: provincial tourism GDP and jobs need an approved method (section 2.5) and no one holds a single view of visitor behaviour. The data-sharing protocol under objective 18 (I16) is the route to closing the gaps below.[^430]
rewrites.70C35A97: Twenty-eight data gaps stand between the plan and a full baseline. Each has a proposed reporting unit or data holder and a route.
rewrites.07E681A6: Two evaluations bracket the plan: a mid-term review in 2030 (which tests seat growth against the path the target requires) and a terminal evaluation in 2035.
rewrites.31087294: The mid-term review tests whether the plan is on its path and whether the path still holds. It falls in 2030 (before runway relief on the planning date) and tests seat growth against the path the target requires. The review also falls at the end of Wesgro's FY26 to FY30 plan period, in time to inform the next one. The terminal evaluation in 2035 measures the result against both cases and sets up the next plan. Both should be run by a party independent of the programme office.[^431]
rewrites.2C20773A: Each goal carries two evaluation questions, one on results and one on the assumptions behind them. For Reshape demand: did arrivals, spend per visitor and green-season nights and share move with the activation and in which markets and segments? Is conversion still the constraint or has access overtaken it in the growth markets? For Transform supply: did seats, readiness and bookability rise outside the Metro and did visitors follow? Did the airport relief arrive on time and did the second gateways carry the load meanwhile? For Build enabling capability: did the pilots meet their thresholds and did community spend rise? Did the national asks get answers and did the data protocol deliver the baselines?
rewrites.53228F7C: The four files are the indicator register, the baseline workbook, the scorecard template and the dashboard data model (SLA clauses 1.1.10.2 and 1.1.15.3). The indicator register holds all 80 indicators with their definition, unit, source, frequency, reporting unit or data holder, baseline and target by year and case. The baseline workbook holds the baseline values with page references to the deliverables and the computed values with their method. Wesgro Research owns both. The programme office owns the scorecard template, which carries the quarterly Steerco scorecard and the annual Board outlook. It also owns the dashboard data model: the feeds, refresh frequency and manual-entry forms for the dashboard in section 5.5.
